sections.html:
A Bethlehem sale runs through an agreement of sale, a city housing inspection, settlement and a recorded deed. The city inspection is the step that surprises most sellers. Your parcel may sit in Northampton County or, on the West Side, in Lehigh County, and that decides which recorder of deeds and which assessment office you deal with. Confirm the county on your tax bill before you list.

The city is a separate jurisdiction from Bethlehem Township, which runs its own resale program. A house inside the city limits follows the city rules below.

Bethlehem is a Lehigh River city of roughly 79,600 people, with an estimate of 79,644 for July 2025, up 5.1 percent from 75,781 in April 2020. It has five areas: Center City, the West Side, the East Side, the South Side and the North Side. Only the West Side lies in Lehigh County.

Owners and renters are close to an even split, with 49.9 percent of homes owner-occupied for 2020 through 2024. The typical owned home is valued at $260,400, median gross rent is $1,382 a month, and median household income is $68,879. There are 31,052 households averaging 2.30 people. Because about half of households rent, many houses that change hands in the city have been rentals at some point, which makes the rental license rules below relevant to a lot of sellers.

sections.h2: The city inspection before title passes
sections.html:
Under Article 119 of the city's codified ordinances, every transferor of real property must have the city's Housing Inspections Bureau inspect it before title passes, and the rule covers residential and commercial property alike. The inspection checks the house against the International Property Maintenance Code and the uses the zoning ordinance allows.

Ordinance 2026-19 amended the requirement in July 2026. The table summarizes the current text of section 119.04.

RequirementWhat section 119.04 provides
When to callWithin 10 days of offering the property for sale
Lead timeBook the inspection a month or more ahead of the transfer
ReportLists uncorrected housing, building, safety or fire violations, plus zoning classification and legality of use
Who gets itGiven to the buyer and attached to the agreement of sale, with any notice of assessment for public improvements
Buyer's dutyBuyer must still obtain a certificate of occupancy
Penalty (section 119.99)Fine of $600 or up to 90 days in jail, or both

The bureau takes scheduling calls Monday through Friday at (610) 865-7091 or (610) 865-7097.

sections.h2: What happens after the inspector writes it up
sections.html:
The report lists whatever housing, building, safety or fire items are uncorrected. It goes to the buyer as an addendum to the agreement of sale. The buyer still has to obtain a certificate of occupancy, so sellers often repair the listed items first, or negotiate in the contract who will do it.

A cash buyer gets the same report. Paying cash does not skip the inspection, so call the bureau within 10 days of offering the house, whoever ends up buying it.

Pick a route by weighing the repair list against your deadline. All three still require you to book the city inspection and give the buyer its report.

  • List with an agent: the widest buyer pool, with showings, repairs ahead of the inspection and a closing date set by the buyer's financing.
  • Sell it yourself: you keep the agent's fee, but you handle the agreement of sale, the city report and the disclosures on your own.
  • Take a cash offer: buyers who pay cash usually buy as is and close on a date you agree, which suits a house with open violations, tenants or deferred repairs.

Compare offers on the net you keep after repairs, taxes and any city-required fixes, not only on the headline price.

Every residential rental unit in Bethlehem needs a rental license each year, and Article 1738 puts rental units on an inspection cycle of once every three years. A landlord who sells should find out where the license stands before listing, because a buyer who plans to keep tenants will ask for the license and the last inspection record.

Rooming houses need an annual inspection under Article 1735, and properties occupied by students or unrelated people fall under Article 1739. When a tenant lives in the house, plan the sale inspection around their access and notice rights, and ask the Housing Inspections Bureau whether your license is current before you list.

The state takes a 1 percent realty transfer tax on the value changing hands, and both seller and buyer are on the hook for it under state law. The recording office collects it together with any local transfer tax when the deed is filed.

Bethlehem's local tax comes from Article 335, which starts at 1 percent and halves the city's piece whenever another taxing body, such as the school district, levies on the same transfer. So the combined local rate on a Bethlehem deed turns on how those two split it. Whichever county recorder handles your parcel, Lehigh or Northampton, keeps a 2 percent commission and sends the rest to the city. Ask that office for the full figure on your deed before you set a price. Close relatives in certain cases, and property that passes by succession, are excluded.

The recorder of deeds for Northampton County or Lehigh County records the deed, depending on where the parcel sits. Section 119.04 also asks every buyer to give the City Engineer a description of the property within one month of acquiring title and to have the deed stamped as proof of registration. Mention it to your buyer early, so the step does not slip once the keys change hands.

Assessment appeals go to the county that assesses the parcel. Call the Northampton County Assessment Division or the Lehigh County assessment office for the current annual appeal filing date, since each office sets its own.

1. Confirm the county on your tax bill and whether the house sits in the city or the township.
  2. Within 10 days of offering the house for sale, call the Housing Inspections Bureau.
  3. Book the inspection a month or more before the transfer date.
  4. Fix the listed items or agree in writing who will.
  5. Attach the report to the agreement of sale for the buyer.
  6. Get the transfer tax total from the recorder of deeds, and close.

faqs.q: Do I need a city inspection if I sell to a cash buyer?
faqs.a: Yes. All properties must be inspected before title transfers, whatever the buyer's financing. Call the Housing Inspections Bureau within 10 days of offering the house, and plan for the report to go to the buyer.

faqs.q: How early should I schedule the Bethlehem sale inspection?
faqs.a: A month or more before the transfer date, and within 10 days of first offering the property for sale. Booking early leaves time to fix any housing, safety or fire items the inspector lists.

faqs.q: What happens if the inspection finds violations?
faqs.a: The report lists them and goes to the buyer as an addendum to the agreement of sale. The buyer must still obtain a certificate of occupancy, so many sellers repair the items first or negotiate who will.

faqs.q: Who bears the transfer tax on a Bethlehem sale?
faqs.a: The agreement of sale decides who pays, but state law makes both seller and buyer liable. The recorder of deeds collects the state tax and the local share at recording.

faqs.q: Which county records my Bethlehem deed?
faqs.a: Northampton County for most of the city. A parcel on the West Side is in Lehigh County and is recorded there. Check the county on your tax bill or assessment record before you schedule settlement.
